place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门 · 执事房
place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the steward's office

setup.zh: 你输了，就不能进下一轮。可那天晌午歇场，周衡把你叫进了执事房：「外门大比，有一条规矩。你知道么？」
setup.en: Lose, and you can't go on. But at the midday break Zhou Heng calls you into the stewards' office: "The contest has a rule. Do you know it?"

recap.zh: 你输了第一轮。晌午歇场，周衡从抽屉里一块一块数出十块灵石：巡夜有功——正好买一次「复试」。
recap.en: You lost the first round. At the midday break Zhou Heng counted ten stones out of his drawer: merit on night watch — exactly the price of a second trial.

en: The midday break, the stewards' office.
On the table, that half candle.

story.zh:
孙二狗的第二轮，对手是柴房那天夜里的五个人里的一个——秘境里抄着手跟在小满身后、给马小宝报信的那一个，崖上饿了三天，这口气还没出。他上台以后，连架势都懒得摆，只把手往背后一背，冲台下马小宝那边笑了一笑，道：「来吧。」孙二狗闭着眼睛冲上去，那人侧身一让，伸脚一勾，他便扑倒在青石板上，下巴磕出了血。

他爬起来了，又冲上去，又扑倒。那人不急着把他推下台，偏往台心上赶，推倒了，等他爬起来，再推倒。台下起先还笑，喊着「二狗，认输吧」「你娘的护身符不管用啦」；到第五回，笑声便稀了；第六回，那人趁他爬到一半，一脚踩在他手背上，碾了一碾，台下有人「嘶」地抽了一口冷气。马小宝在台下拍手：「好！踩得好！谁叫他跟沈小满好！」

小满站在台下，一句话也没说。他的手在袖子里攥着，攥得指甲掐进了肉里。五扇门后头那一圈光，给这一脚踩得往上一窜，窜到他喉咙口，烫得他眼睛发酸。他只要往台上跨一步——一步，那个人便要在半空里转三个圈。可跨了这一步，全外门便都看见了：一个验过修为、名册上写着二层的人，一步跨上台，一掌打飞了一个三层的老弟子。胸口的木牌凉凉的，一个很困的声音，只说了一个字：「藏。」

他没有跨。第七回，孙二狗扶着膝盖站起来，满脸是血，腰里那个蓝布包的绳子断了一根，吊在胯骨边上晃荡。他伸手把它捞起来，塞回腰带里，又冲着那人走了过去——不是冲，是走，一步一步，腿抖得跟筛糠一样，每一步都踩得实实在在。执事敲响了铜锣：「停。孙二狗，你还能打么？」孙二狗吐出一口血沫子：「……能。」执事道：「我看不能了。」孙二狗想了想，点点头：「……那就不能了。」他冲执事鞠了一躬，冲那人也鞠了一躬，自己走下了台子。

他没让人扶，一直走到演武场边上那几级石阶跟前，一屁股坐了下去，坐下去便再也站不起来了。小满走过去，在他面前站了一会儿，伸出手去：「起来。地上凉。」孙二狗抓住他的手，他一使劲，把他拉了起来。孙二狗比他高半个头，瘦得一把骨头，拉起来的时候，轻飘飘的，像拉起一根竹竿。九月初九那天，石阶的一百四十级上，有一个兖州来的孩子坐着起不来，小满从他身边走了过去，没有停。他那时想，等我站得够稳了，我要拉。今天他也不算站得多稳，可好歹拉了一个。

那一上午，五行台上打了两轮。秦雁上台两回，剑都没出鞘，拿剑鞘一点一拨，两个对手便自己走下了台。马小宝也上台两回，镜子挂在腰里，没摘，一拳一个，拳头砸在青石板上，石板上留下两个白印子。一夜两层的力气，是真的。他站在台上，冲台下的小满扬了扬下巴。

晌午歇场。周衡站到五行台上，翻开那本蓝布面的名录，清了清嗓子，照着念道：「外门大比规矩，第十七条：输了第一轮的，可纳灵石十块，复试一场。复试者，挑当届名册上排头一人；胜，入决赛，被挑者出局；负，逐下台，灵石不退。」念完了，他从怀里摸出一根香，插在台角的香炉里，点着了，「歇场一炷香。要复试的，香烧完之前，灵石交到执事房。」他又补了一句：「这一条，设了三十年，一回都没人用过。」

台下静了一静，跟着便嗡的一声，一齐转过头来看小满。马小宝的声音从人堆里拔了出来：「他？他拿什么交？他连一块灵石都掏不出来！」一片哄笑。小满站在那里，脸上火辣辣的。他怀里一块灵石也没有；有过的，都叫这口水缸一口一口地喝干了。

他还是去了执事房。周衡坐在桌后，桌上点着半根蜡烛——他的蜡烛向来只点半根，另外半根掰下来收在抽屉里。小满说：「周师兄，我想复试。」周衡道：「十块。」小满说：「我没有。」周衡看了他一眼，低下头去翻账簿：「规矩是规矩。没有，就没有。」

小满站了一会儿，出了门。马小宝正倚在执事房门口，手里抛着一块灵石，一抛一接，见他出来，把那块灵石往他脚跟前一扔：「捡呀。一块。还差九块。」旁边几个跟班哄地笑了。那块灵石在泥地里滚了两滚，停在小满的草鞋尖上。小满低头看了它一眼，抬脚从它旁边迈了过去。马小宝在他身后道：「沈小满，今年的丹，姓马。」台角那炷香，烧下去一半了。石阶上，孙二狗下巴上贴着伙房大娘给的膏药，贴歪了，他冲小满咧了咧嘴，嘴里还有血。老槐树底下，钱掌柜正拿炭条把「沈小满」后头的「一赔一百」划了，要往上改，想了想，又把炭条放下了——一个输了第一轮、又交不起十块灵石的人，赔率没法往上写了，写多少都是零。

阿禾比他先到了槐树底下。她把那张折成一小块的纸条拍在秤盘上：「掌柜的，我押的那一文，退给我。」钱掌柜抬起眼皮：「押了就是押了。板上写的，就是我说的——押出去的，不退。」阿禾道：「我拿它有急用。」钱掌柜道：「急用也不退。今天给你退了，明天人人来退，我这块板子，就不干净了。」阿禾咬着嘴唇，站了一会儿，没再说话。

阿禾回过头来，看见了小满。她什么也没说，把纸条收回本子里，从他身边走了过去。小满知道她要那一文做什么：一文钱，离十块灵石，差着十万八千里；可她身上，只有那一文。

小满在老槐树底下站住了。他袖子里有一个小瓷瓶，伙房扔的那只辣椒油瓶子，他自己在井边洗了七遍，瓶里一颗丹，饭桶第二炉出的回春丹，九道金纹。那是留给他爹的膝盖的——他爹的膝盖，逢阴天便「聊天」，逢下雨便「报天气」，一辈子跪人跪坏的。这一颗拿到钱掌柜的秤盘上，莫说十块灵石，一百块也换得来。可一颗九道金纹的丹，外门没有一个人见过；拿出去，头一个问的便是「哪来的」——这一问，他答不上来，饭桶便藏不住了，银月也藏不住了。他攥着那个瓶子，攥得瓶身都热了，到底没有掏出来。
story.en:
Sun Ergou's second round was against one of the five from the woodshed night — the one who'd trailed Xiaoman with folded arms in the hidden realm and run to tell Ma Xiaobao, starved three days on the cliff, the grudge still in him. On the stage he didn't even take a stance; he put his hands behind his back, smiled toward Ma Xiaobao below, and said: "Come on." Sun Ergou charged with his eyes shut; the man stepped aside and hooked a foot, and Sun Ergou went flat on the bluestone and split his chin.

He got up, charged again, fell again. The man wasn't in a hurry to push him off; he herded him toward the centre, knocked him down, waited for him to get up, knocked him down again. At first the crowd laughed and shouted, "Ergou, give up!" "Your ma's charm's no good!"; by the fifth time the laughter thinned; the sixth time, as he was halfway up, the man stepped on the back of his hand and ground it, and someone below sucked in a breath. Ma Xiaobao clapped: "Good! Nice stomp! That's what you get for being Shen Xiaoman's friend!"

Xiaoman stood below and said nothing. His hands were clenched in his sleeves till the nails bit his palms. The ring of light behind his five doors, kicked by that stomp, surged up into his throat, so hot his eyes stung. He had only to take one step onto the stage — one step, and that man would turn three times in the air. But take that step, and the whole outer court would see: a boy checked at layer two, written layer two in the register, stepping up and knocking a layer-three senior flying with one palm. The token on his chest was cool, and a very sleepy voice said just one word: "Hide."

He didn't step. The seventh time, Sun Ergou pushed himself up by his knees, face all blood, one string of the blue pouch snapped so it dangled at his hip. He caught it, tucked it back in his belt, and went at the man again — not charging, walking, one step at a time, legs shaking like a sieve, every step planted firm. The steward struck the gong: "Stop. Sun Ergou, can you go on?" Sun Ergou spat a mouthful of bloody froth: "…I can." "I say you can't." Sun Ergou thought, and nodded: "…Then I can't." He bowed to the steward, bowed to the man too, and walked down off the stage by himself.

He let no one help him, walked all the way to the few steps at the edge of the ground and sat down hard, and once down he couldn't get up again. Xiaoman went over, stood before him a moment, and held out his hand: "Up. The ground's cold." Sun Ergou took it and Xiaoman pulled him up. Sun Ergou was half a head taller and nothing but bones; pulled up, he weighed nothing, like pulling up a bamboo pole. On the ninth of the ninth month, at the hundred-and-fortieth step, a boy from Yan had sat unable to get up, and Xiaoman had walked past without stopping. He'd thought then: when I stand steady enough, I'll pull. Today he wasn't standing all that steady either, but at least he'd pulled one.

That morning two rounds were fought on the platform. Qin Yan went up twice and never drew her sword; she tapped and nudged with the scabbard and both opponents walked off the stage by themselves. Ma Xiaobao went up twice too, the mirror left hanging at his waist, one punch each, and his fists left two white marks in the bluestone. The strength of two layers in one night was real. He stood on the stage and jerked his chin at Xiaoman below.

The midday break. Zhou Heng stood on the platform, opened the blue register, cleared his throat and read: "Rules of the outer court contest, article seventeen: one who loses the first round may pay ten spirit stones for a second trial. The challenger takes on the one standing first on this year's register; if he wins, he goes to the final and the one challenged is out; if he loses, he is sent down, stones not refunded." When he'd read it he took a stick of incense from his coat, stuck it in the burner at the corner of the stage and lit it. "The break is one stick. Whoever wants a second trial, stones to the stewards' office before it burns out." And he added: "This article was set thirty years ago. Nobody's ever used it."

A moment's silence below, then a hum, and every head turned to Xiaoman. Ma Xiaobao's voice rose out of the crowd: "Him? Pay with what? He can't even scrape up one stone!" A burst of laughter. Xiaoman stood there, his face burning. He hadn't a single stone on him; whatever he'd had, this water vat had drunk dry mouthful by mouthful.

He went to the stewards' office anyway. Zhou Heng sat behind the table; on it burned half a candle — he only ever burned half, the other half broken off and kept in the drawer. "Brother Zhou, I want the second trial." "Ten." "I haven't got it." Zhou Heng glanced at him and went back to his ledger: "Rules are rules. If you haven't, you haven't."

Xiaoman stood a moment and went out. Ma Xiaobao was leaning by the door, tossing a stone and catching it; seeing him he threw it at his heels: "Pick it up. One. Nine to go." The followers roared. The stone rolled twice in the mud and stopped at the toe of Xiaoman's sandal. He looked at it and stepped over it. Behind him Ma Xiaobao said: "Shen Xiaoman, this year's pill is named Ma." The incense on the corner of the stage had burned halfway. On the steps Sun Ergou, a plaster from the kitchen auntie stuck crooked on his chin, grinned at him with blood still in his mouth. Under the pagoda tree Money-Keeper Qian was crossing out the "one to a hundred" after Shen Xiaoman with his charcoal, meaning to raise it; he thought, and put the charcoal down — a boy who'd lost the first round and couldn't pay ten stones had no odds worth writing; whatever you wrote, it came to nothing.

A He had got to the pagoda tree before him. She slapped the little folded slip down on the scale pan: "Shopkeeper, the one cash I bet — give it back." Qian raised his eyelids: "A bet is a bet. What's on the board is what I said — once it's bet, it's not returned." "I need it urgently." "Urgent or not, no. Give it back to you today and tomorrow everyone comes for theirs, and this board of mine isn't clean any more." A He bit her lip, stood a while, and said no more.

A He turned and saw Xiaoman. She said nothing, put the slip back in her notebook and walked past him. Xiaoman knew what she'd wanted the cash for: one cash, and ten spirit stones a world away from it; but one cash was all she had.

Under the pagoda tree Xiaoman stopped. In his sleeve was a little porcelain bottle — the chilli-oil bottle the kitchen threw out, which he had washed seven times at the well himself — and in it one pill, a healing pill from the rice-bucket's second batch, nine gold lines. It was for his father's knees — the knees that chatted when it was overcast and gave the forecast when it rained, worn out from a lifetime of kneeling to people. On Money-Keeper Qian's scale it would fetch not ten stones but a hundred. But no one in the outer court had ever seen a pill with nine gold lines; bring it out, and the first question would be where from — and he couldn't answer that, and the rice-bucket couldn't stay hidden, and nor could Yinyue. He gripped the bottle a long time, till it was warm in his hand, and in the end didn't take it out.

story.zh:
小满又进了执事房。这一回，他没等周衡抬头，便道：「周师兄，我拿明年的残株抵。」周衡的笔停了。小满道：「药园每月拔下来的残株，你说往年都是扔，往后扔给我。明年一年，十二篮，我一根不要，都抵给你。十块灵石，够不够？」

他说这话的时候，心口疼得厉害。那十二篮残株，旁人眼里是垃圾，在柴房那只饭桶嘴里，却是一炉一炉的丹——那是他往后一年里唯一的料。这一句话出口，等于把自己明年的路，押在了今天这一场上。

周衡看着他。蜡烛的火苗子一跳一跳的。他道：「残株是垃圾。垃圾，不抵账。」小满的心往下一沉。周衡却拉开了抽屉，从里头拿出一样东西放在桌上——正是那掰下来的半根蜡烛。跟着翻开账簿，拿指头点着一行一行往下念：「十月初一至初九，药园丢灵草十株。初十起，沈小满巡夜，至今一株没丢，外加灵兽一只，狰，入册。另议的那一笔，今天议——」他从抽屉里一块一块地往外数，数一块，拿笔在账上划一道，「——一、二、三……十块。」数完了，又道：「记账。」

小满看着那十块灵石，又看看那半根蜡烛：「周师兄，这一笔……不是说腊八才结？」周衡翻账簿的手停了一停，道：「账上欠你的。十月上旬丢了十株，你接手以后，一株没丢——十株，十块。腊八结账，早上说过了。」他把账簿合上，「用过人家的，一定要还。连猫的账，都结。」小满把灵石揣进怀里，走到门口，回过头来叫了一声：「……周师兄。」周衡道：「嗯。」小满说：「有前途。」周衡咳嗽一声，挥挥手，叫他滚了。小满出了门，听见身后执事房里「咔」的一声轻响，大约是周衡又把那半根蜡烛掰回了抽屉里。台角那炷香，还剩一指。

复试，挑名册上排头一个。排头一个，是秦雁。周衡把第十七条又念了一遍，念到「被挑者出局」，台下一片哗然：她上午两场都赢了，这一场要是输了，三年的队便白排了；赢了，也不过是回到原地。周衡看着她：「秦雁，你接不接？」规矩上她不能不接，周衡却还是问了。秦雁道：「接。」

台角的水缸边上，两个人碰上了。秦雁舀了半瓢水，没喝，递给了他。小满接过来喝了，道：「秦师姐。秘境里那一回……」秦雁道：「你没往下坠。我记得。」她又舀了一瓢，自己喝了，望着台上那炷香，「你知道我为什么排了三年？」小满摇头。秦雁道：「进了内门，一月十块灵石，能折银子寄家。我爹前年叫熊把腿咬了，躺到如今。今年是我排头。」她把瓢放回缸沿上，「你这一场赢了，我明年再排；你这一场输了，十块灵石是周衡的——他那一笔『另议』，我也听说了。」她看着他，「我不让你。你也别让我。」

小满捧着那瓢，半天没说出话来。他想说「我不上了」，话到嘴边，想起那十二篮残株，想起孙二狗石阶上那一口血，又咽了回去。他把瓢放下，冲她抱了抱拳。秦雁点了点头，先上了台。
story.en:
Xiaoman went back into the office. This time he didn't wait for Zhou Heng to look up: "Brother Zhou, I'll pledge next year's culls." Zhou Heng's brush stopped. "The culls pulled from the herb garden each month — you said you used to throw them out, and now you'd throw them to me. Next year, twelve baskets; I won't take a single stalk, I'll pledge them all to you. Is that good for ten stones?"

As he said it his heart ached badly. Those twelve baskets were rubbish to anyone else; in the mouth of the rice-bucket in the woodshed they were batch after batch of pills — his only feedstock for the year to come. Saying it meant staking next year's road on today's bout.

Zhou Heng looked at him. The candle flame jumped. "Culls are rubbish. Rubbish doesn't settle accounts." Xiaoman's heart sank. But Zhou Heng opened the drawer and took something out and set it on the table — the very half candle he'd broken off. Then he opened the ledger and read down it with a finger: "First to ninth of the tenth month, herb garden, ten herbs lost. From the tenth, Shen Xiaoman on night watch; not one lost since, and one spirit beast, a zheng, entered in the register. The 'to be settled' — settled today." He counted stones out of the drawer one at a time, striking a line in the ledger for each: "— one, two, three… ten." Then he said: "On the books."

Xiaoman looked at the ten stones, then at the half candle. "Brother Zhou, this… didn't you say accounts close on Laba?" Zhou Heng's hand paused on the ledger. "The books owe you. Ten lost in the first ten days of the tenth month; since you took over, not one — ten herbs, ten stones. Accounts close on Laba; I said so this morning." He closed the ledger. "What you've used of others, you repay. Even the cats' accounts get settled." Xiaoman pocketed the stones, went to the door, turned and called: "…Brother Zhou." "Mm." "Promising," said Xiaoman. Zhou Heng coughed and waved him out. Outside the door Xiaoman heard a soft snap from the office — likely Zhou Heng breaking the half candle back into the drawer. The incense on the stage had one finger left.

The second trial: take on the one standing first on the register. First on the register was Qin Yan. Zhou Heng read article seventeen again, and at "the one challenged is out" the crowd erupted: she had won both her bouts that morning; lose this one and her three years of queuing were for nothing; win it, and she was only back where she'd been. Zhou Heng looked at her: "Qin Yan, do you accept?" By the rules she couldn't refuse, and still Zhou Heng asked. "I accept," said Qin Yan.

By the water vat at the corner of the stage the two of them met. Qin Yan ladled half a scoop and didn't drink it; she handed it to him. Xiaoman drank. "Sister Qin. That time in the hidden realm…" "You didn't hang. I remember." She ladled another and drank it herself, watching the incense on the stage. "Do you know why I've queued three years?" Xiaoman shook his head. "In the inner court it's ten stones a month, and you can change them into silver and send it home. Two years ago a bear took my father's leg; he's been lying down ever since. This year I'm first in line." She set the ladle on the vat's rim. "If you win this bout, I queue again next year; if you lose, the ten stones are Zhou Heng's — I've heard about his 'to be settled' too." She looked at him. "I won't give way to you. Don't you give way to me."

Xiaoman held the ladle and couldn't say a word for a long time. He wanted to say, "I won't go up"; it got as far as his lips, and then he thought of the twelve baskets of culls, and of the mouthful of blood on the steps from Sun Ergou, and swallowed it. He set the ladle down and saluted her. Qin Yan nodded and went up onto the stage first.
